passage: At the school's annual day, Afreen waved from the parents' rows when Parul came off stage. Parul, fourteen, looked straight past her. Later in the canteen, Afreen reached to fix her daughter's hair clip; Parul ducked away, rolled her eyes and said, "Ammi, not here," then went to join her friends. Afreen's throat tightened. She felt like an embarrassing stranger. At the tea counter another mother, Zohra, smiled at her. "Mine's sixteen. It's them growing up, not leaving. Just stay nearby." So Afreen didn't follow. She sat on the bench by the school gate with two cups of tea and texted only: "You were brilliant tonight. I'm by the gate whenever you're ready." A while later Parul dropped onto the bench beside her, took a cup and said, "Did you see when I nearly tripped?"

qa.q: Where did Afreen wait?
qa.a: On the bench by the school gate.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling when Parul ducked away?
qa.a: She felt hurt and rejected, like an embarrassing stranger to her own daughter.

qa.q: What did Afreen choose, and why did it work?
qa.a: She stayed nearby without following or pushing and sent a warm text, which kept the door open so Parul came to her.

qa.q: Why might Parul have ducked away in the canteen?
qa.a: She probably felt embarrassed being fussed over in front of friends and wanted to seem grown up, rather than rejecting her mother.

grounding: Shows a parent feeling rejected by a teenager's sudden distance and eye-rolling, and staying available without pressure so the door stays open.

passage:
Dear Amma,
You asked on the phone why I sounded low. It's Vijay. A few months ago my son told me everything; now he answers in one word, keeps his door shut and rolls his eyes if I ask about school. On Sunday I knocked with chai and he said, "Can you not?" and closed the door. I cried in the kitchen, Amma. I felt I had lost him. Then I remembered myself at his age, a girl hiding on the terrace with my diary, and how you never forced my door, you just left the kitchen light on. So I've stopped pushing. I sit in the living room in the evenings with my book and ask nothing. Last night he came and sat at the other end of the sofa and told me about a cricket match. I'm holding on to that.
Your Vinita

qa.q: What did Vijay say when Vinita knocked with chai?
qa.a: "Can you not?"

qa.q: How did Vinita feel after the door closed?
qa.a: She felt rejected and sad, crying in the kitchen as if she had lost him.

qa.q: What did Vinita change, and why is it wise?
qa.a: She stopped pushing and simply stayed available in the living room, which let Vijay come to her in his own time.

qa.q: What might Vijay's need for privacy mean from his side?
qa.a: It is likely a normal part of growing up and pulling away a little, not a rejection of his mother.

grounding: Illustrates a parent hurt by a teenager's sudden wish for privacy and short replies, and staying available without pressure to keep the door open.

Kashish: k

qa.q: What was for dinner?
qa.a: Rajma, at 8.

qa.q: What did Madhuri feel when Kashish asked to eat alone?

qa.q: What did Madhuri do that kept the door open?

qa.a: Kashish seems to want closeness on Kashish's own terms, without being questioned.

grounding: Shows a parent hurt by a teen's sudden distance who stays available without pressure, so the teen comes back when ready.

passage: Mridul used to sit on the counter of Nirmala's small grocery shop in Ranikhet after school, chattering about cricket and eating peanuts from the sack. This year he walked straight past with his earphones in, rolled his eyes when she asked about his day, and slammed the door of his room behind the shop. One evening she stood outside that door with a plate of pakoras, her throat tight. Had she done something wrong? The neighbour, weighing out sugar, said, "My son was the same at fifteen. They come back." So Nirmala stopped knocking and asking. She just left the pakoras on his desk and kept the shop light on late. Two weeks later Mridul drifted to the counter at closing time, sat down, and started talking about a girl in his class who was "so annoying". Nirmala kept counting coins and listened.

qa.q: What did Nirmala leave on Mridul's desk?
qa.a: The pakoras.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling outside Mridul's door?
qa.a: She felt hurt and anxious, throat tight, wondering if she had done something wrong.

qa.q: What helped keep the door open?
qa.a: Dropping the pressure of knocking and questions, while staying available with food and the shop light on late.

qa.q: How might Mridul see his mother's questions this year?
qa.a: He seems to want privacy and space, so questions may feel intrusive, even though he still comes back to talk.

grounding: Shows a parent hurt by a teen's eye-rolling and slammed doors who stays available without pressure until the teen returns.

passage: Alejandro used to drive Liam to football every Saturday, the two of them singing badly to old Spanish songs. This autumn Liam asked to be dropped a street away from the pitch. At home he answered in grunts, spent evenings behind a closed door, and once said, "Can you not come to the match? It's embarrassing." Alejandro laughed it off, then sat in the car in the dark driveway for twenty minutes, stung. On the phone, his sister reminded him what he'd been like at fourteen. So he stopped asking about the match. He kept the Saturday drive, a street away, and left the radio on their old station without comment. In November, stuck in traffic, Liam started humming along. Then he said, "Dad, can I ask you something about a friend?" Alejandro turned the music down and kept his eyes on the road.

qa.q: Where did Liam ask to be dropped?
qa.a: A street away from the pitch.

qa.q: What was Alejandro feeling in the dark driveway?
qa.a: He felt stung and rejected after Liam called his coming to the match embarrassing.

qa.q: What did Alejandro do that kept the door open?
qa.a: He stopped pushing about the match but kept the Saturday drive and the old radio station, staying available without pressure.

qa.q: How might Liam see his dad at the match?
qa.a: Liam may feel embarrassed in front of friends and want some independence, rather than wanting to reject his dad.

grounding: Shows a parent stung by a teen's sudden distance who keeps a quiet, pressure-free routine until the teen opens up again.

passage: At the parent-teacher meeting, Sarika walked three steps ahead of her father and rolled her eyes when Pankaj waved at her friends. In the classroom she answered her teacher in full sentences but gave him only shrugs. On the way out, Pankaj stood by the notice board, stung. 'At home too,' he said quietly to the class teacher. 'Door shut, earphones in. She used to tell me everything.' The teacher smiled. 'She's kind in class and working hard. Pulling away from parents at this age is usually normal. Just stay easy to find.' That evening Pankaj left a cup of hot chocolate outside her door with a note: 'No questions. Here if you want to talk.' An hour later she came out and sat beside him watching cricket, saying nothing. It was enough.

qa.q: What did Pankaj leave outside Sarika's door?
qa.a: A cup of hot chocolate with a note.

qa.q: How did Pankaj feel by the notice board?
qa.a: He felt stung and rejected, missing the daughter who used to tell him everything.

qa.q: What did the class teacher advise, and how did Pankaj use it?
qa.a: To stay easy to find without pressure; Pankaj left a no-questions note offering to talk.

qa.q: What might Sarika have felt about her father waving at her friends?
qa.a: She probably felt embarrassed and wanted some independence, which does not mean she stopped loving him.

grounding: A father hurt by his teenage daughter's sudden distance learns it is normal and stays available without pressure.
